messages.subject: point counts and snapshots
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
=20
I have been using distance sampling for years to census birds and have
become increasingly interested in the problems associated with point
counts, particularly the issue of movement and positive bias in
population estimates.  I have looked through the archives regarding this
topic and spoke with Len Thomas and David Borchers about the issue at
the Distance Sampling Workshops in Canada about a month ago.  The
snapshot idea is really interesting, and I am going to try to
incorporate it into point counts I'm working on.
=20
My question is about determining the snapshot and incorporating it into
analyses.  Obviously, the appropriate snapshot length will vary
depending on several factors including habitat and species, but once a
snapshot time is determined, could this amount of time simply be divided
into a longer point count and accounted for in survey effort?   For
example if an observer determines that the appropriate time frame for a
snapshot is 1 minute, why couldn't that person simply conduct a 5 minute
point count and enter the survey effort in as 5 in Distance?  I am
uncomfortable with this approach, but I'm not sure why.  Is there an
assumption of independence (relating to time between surveys) involved
with survey effort? =20
=20
Like many folks, I would like to be able to estimate abundances (1) as
accurately as possible for (2) as many species as possible.  The effect
of time places these two goals at odds.  The removal model described in
Pollock et al. 2002 is worth considering, but it would be more
straightforward and analytically easier if the survey effort idea I
suggest above could work.
=20
Your thoughts and insights are much appreciated!
=20
Alison Styring

messages.subject: Re: point counts and snapshots
messages.body_plain:
Alison, strictly, the snapshot method is literally that - an instant in
time.  Of course, you need to spend some time ahead of the snapshot
moment, getting to grips with what is around you, and some time after the
moment, verifying where birds were.  You could in principle have more than
one snapshot moment per point.  Generally, I would advise against this,
especially with only a minute between snapshot moments, as I suspect it
would compromise data quality in high density areas - though it may be
workable for say single-species surveys.  Whether you would gain much
benefit depends on the extent to which birds move around.  If they move
around a lot, more than one snapshot at a visit might potentially be
useful, but generally, I suspect the additional information content would
be slight, and not worthwhile.

The problem with the removal model is that it does not model a major
source of heterogeneity in the detectabilities - that due to distance from
the point - and we know the removal method is strongly biased in this
circumstance.  Their reason for ignoring this was that many birders are
adamant that they cannot measure detection distances.  My own view is that
we should try to change that perception, rather than develop methodologies
that we know are subject to bias.  The argument that they only want
relative estimates of abundance doesn't hold up, because the bias is not
consistent across species, habitats, time, etc., so trends in time or
space are biased, and comparisons across species invalid.

Last month, I tried 4 different approaches out:  5-minute counts, the
snapshot method, a method based on cues (estimate number of songbursts per
unit area per unit time, and convert this to an estimate of number of
birds, using a separate estimate of the cue (song) rate, and line transect
sampling.  I found that line transect sampling was the easiest to
implement, and gave highest precision - but in many sites, random lines
are impossible to navigate.  The snapshot method proved very workable, and
took less time than the 5-minute count approach.  Of the 4 species I
concentrated on, the 5-minute count method appreciably overestimated the
density of one species, whereas the snapshot method showed no evidence of
bias.  The cue-based method makes no assumption about movement.  It was
workable for 4 species, but if I had been recording all species, I would
have been swamped, try to record distances for each separate
cue.  Estimates seemed unbiased, but precision was lower than for other
methods.  Estimation of distance, using a laser rangefinder, presented few
problems, even though perhaps 90% of detected birds were not visible.
However, the woodland was for the most part fairly open.  I am in the
process of writing this up.

The advanced distance sampling book, due out around August, also describes
the cue-based method, and discusses the removal model.

Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hello list,

Continuing with the avian point count theme, I am on the verge of abandoning my
plans to use distance sampling for this summer's field work and instead just
spot map, or more likely do both. I am studying the distribution of early-
successional shrubland bird species in relation to habitat factors in about 60
discrete patches scattered across a large forested landscape. These patches
range in size from 0.1 to 10 ha.  Ideally, I would like an estimate of density
for all common species in each patch, or at least for smaller plots within each
patch. My understanding is that distance sampling will not allow for this
(unless I visited each patch many times) because the really small patches often
have only one or two individuals of each species. There is also going to be a
lot of heterogeneity in abundance among sites because of differences in
vegetation structure, patch size etc... Would it be worth my while to try and
model overall density using a lot of covariates in DISTANCE or should I scrap
the distance sampling and go ahead and put in the extra effort spot mapping?

Thanks,
Richard

--

messages.body_plain:
Richard,

One of my students has used distance sampling to look at density of
grassland songbirds in patches (reclaimed surface mines) ranging from 0.5 -
120 ha.  Because we had no reason to suspect detectability differed among
patches of different sizes, she generated a pooled detectability function
across all patches and then applied that detection probability to each
patch.  Yes, there was a lot of variability in density, even among patches
of the same size, but with a large number of patches (~120) she was able to
model a density-area relationship as well as detect various factors (habitat
and landscape characteristics) that were related to species density.

I may be wrong, but I think you are confusing distance sampling's ability to
correct for detection issues with the relationships you are expecting to
find among patch characteristics and species abundance.  If you believe that
detection of birds is NOT related to characteristics of individual patches
then you can simply pool all your observations to generate a global
detection function.  This global detection function can then be applied to
your data from individual patches to obtain density estimates for each
patch.  If you think there are 1 or 2 environmental features that affect
detectability across patches then you might be able to model them as a
covariate - but this is distinct from the characteristics you believe are
related to bird density.

I doubt if the precision for estimates at the individual patch level will be
very good, but repeat visits and having as many points/transects per patch
could help in this regard.  Consequently, it will be important to have a
large number of patches to tease apart any density-habitat relationships.

If you have 60 patches to visit I don't know how you could do enough spot
mapping at each patch to obtain density estimates without an army of people
to assist you.  I think the data you would collect by using distance
sampling would be better for the types of questions you seemed to be
interested in studying.

Hopefully, others on this listserve will have some useful suggestions for
you as you design your project.

Regards,

Duane Diefenbach

In that circumstance, I would favour spot-mapping.  Even for your largest
patches, I think I would favour this, and for patches of 0.1 ha, I don't
think it would be sensible to do any other approach.  My own view is that,
for typical songbird surveys, you need to get up to perhaps 20 or 30 ha

(perhaps because vegetation is very thick), spot-mapping may become
unreliable in smaller sites.  (Distances can also be difficult to estimate
in these circumstances.)

messages.body_plain:
A brief follow-up to Duane's useful comments.  It was the requirement of
abundance estimates by each individual patch that prompted me to suggest
spot-mapping is better.  With very small patches, it is usually fairly
easy to identify waht is present, but distance sampling needs a lot of
effort to get sensible estimates by patch.  There is another issue though
- with such small patches, edge effects can't be ignored.  Objects are no
longer distributed independently of point location, if your sample points
are only within the patches.  You can get around this by putting say a
grid of points down randomly over the whole area spanning all your
patches, then surveying all points that fall within w of any of your
patches, where w is the truncation distance.  This issue (+ sampling) and
related ones are addressed in the advanced distance sampling book, due out
around August.  So distance sampling can be made to work - but I would
generally favour spot-mapping for very small patches.

Steve

messages.subject: Re: Range finder
messages.body_plain:
> > I think this raises a really good question about the ability to measure or

> > indeed accurately estimate distances in dense vegetation. For avian point
> > counts in tropical forest the majority of individuals are heard but not

> > seen, complicating the issue somewhat. Even with training, is it possible to

> > accurately estimate the distance from observer to an unseen calling
> > individual? If not, what's the answer?!

My experience is that you can get inconsistent readings, when trying to
look through say tall grasses or branches of deciduous trees before they
leaf out.  Sometimes you get a reading to the vegetation, and sometimes to
what is beyond.  So long as you're reasonably competent at estimating
distances by eye, it is not difficult to figure out what distance you got.
However, as soon as the vegetation is at all thick, the rangefinder will
give you the distance to it, and not beyond.  My view is that it does not
replace observer training;  the observer has to be able to estimate the
location of unseen birds.  In fairly open woodland, I found this wasn't
difficult;  it was fairly easy usually to determine which tree or patch of
scrub the bird was in, and measure to that.  Also, it is wise to have a
field protocol that allows the observer to verify more problematic
locations, by allowing movement away from the line or point.  For point
transects, this movement might be during the count itself, to help locate
a singing bird or to give a better view (though such movement shouldn't be
excessive, and recorded distances should be to the point), or after the
count has finished for that point (in which more movement is OK).
The methods can tolerate quite a bit of error in distant detections, where
probability of detection is quite low, but good accuracy is needed closer
to the line or point, say where detection probability is around 0.6 or
higher - this is especially true for point transect sampling.

In more closed habitats, the problems are much greater.  Laser
rangefinders are still useful.  For example, trained observers can usually
make a reasonable estimate of where a singing bird is, and even if they
can't see the location, they may be able to see a tree or object at a
similar distance from them, in a slightly different direction.  Accurate
measurement of this guessed distance is better than a guess at the guessed
distance!  Observer training should include setting up trials where the
true distance is known, so that errors can be quantified.

Steve

messages.body_plain:
Hi James,

> >Now, I wish to adjust my counts (number of detections within 100-m radius) to
> >account for variation in detection probability resulting from variation in shrub
> > cover.

The easy way, assuming each point is entered as a sample in Distance, is to set up
a new Model Definition and tick the box to estimate density by sample in the
Estimate tab.  If you want abundance by point, it's simply density*pi*w^2 where w
is truncation distance.

However, if you want to calculate abundance in each sample (point) by hand, you
can use the Horvitz-Thompson-like estimator:
   estimated abundance = sum(1/estimated p_i)
where the sum is over all animals counted at the point, and p_i is the estimated
probability of detecting the ith animal, given it is within the truncation
distance.  To calculate p_i, see the Distance online help -- look in the index
under Detection function, formulae, about.  Note that if you don't have animal
level covariates (which it appears you don't) then p_i will be the same for all
animals at a point, so the above reduces to
   estimated abundance = n/p
where n is the count at the point and p is the estimated probability of detecting
an animal given it is within the truncation distance.

As an aside, assuming that your stands vary in size, then by locating one point in
each stand you have a design with a different proportion of the stand area
surveyed in each point (different "coverage probability" in each stand).  If
you're also interested in calculating an average density over all stands, you'll
need to take this into account.  You could calculate a weighted mean of the stand
densities, with the weight being the proportion of the stand area surveyed.

Hope this helps,

 - Len

Hi James,

I don't think you need to do anything by hand, unless you're a masochist!    I
wasn't 100% clear in my previous message so I'll try to lay it out better here.
For that reason I'm also cc'ing this to the list, in case anyone else wants to
do the same thing.

I think you want to fit the detection function using all your data, but with
habitat as a covariate (which you have done), but then *predict* the probability
of detection at each point, given the habitat type of the point and that the
animal is present within the truncation distance.  You then want to calculate
density (or abundance) at each point using this habitat-specific probability of
detection.

You can do this in the multiple covariate engine of Distance in the Model
Definition | Estimate tab.  Under "Quantities to estimate and level of
resolution", for the Density and the detection function rows, tick both the
"Global" and "Sample" columns.  Make sure you have habitat as a covariate.  For
more about this, see the online help, Chapter 9, Defining MCDS models,
Estimating the detection function at multiple levels.

The output you will get will be density for each point, and p_i for animals at
each point too.  (You will also get abundance for each point, but there's a bug
in Distance where the area used to calculate this is currently wrong so it's
acutally abunance for the whole study area assuming density at that point
applies to the whole study area -- this bug is fixed in the next version of
Distance to be released.)

You *can* calculate probability of detection by hand if you really want to - but
it's going to require some work.  We want p_i, the probability of detecting an
animal at each point, given that it is within the truncation distance.  Note,
this isn't the probability of detecting the animal at it's observed distance --
it's the probability given that the animal was somewhere between 0 and w.  We
could use the observed distances but then estimation tends to be less reliable
-- for more on this see the MCDS chapter of the up-coming Advanced Distance
Sampling book.  Because we're integrating out the distance component, the only
covariate left is habitat, so that means the p_i's will be the same for all
animals at each point, given the amount of shrub cover.  So what you need to do
is program Excel (or something better) to work out probability of detection for
a given covariate level and distance, and then program Excel (or whatever) to
integrate this function between 0 and w, using numerical integration such as
Simpson's rule.  As you can see, it's probably easier to let Distance do it!

Specific replies to your questions about estimating p below, should you still
want to do it.

Cheers,

 - Len

On Thu, 13 May 2004 14:58:43 -0400, Tucker, James wrote:

> >Dr. Thomas:

but I do not have enough observations for most samples (points) to estimate
probability of detection for individual points.  Could you please help me with
the following questions?
> >
> >If I calculate p_i, the estimated probability of detecting the ith animal, will
the mean for the p_i at a point be a good estimate for probability of detection
at that point?

As I explained above, you could do it this way, but better to use the definition
I gave of p_i as probability of detection given the animal is between 0 and w,
rather than probability at a given distance.  In the former case, all p_i's for
each animal at a point are the same (because you have no animal level covariates
other than distance).

> >I do not have animal level covariates, but I want to adjust p_i to account for
the influence of shrub cover at each point.  Does the calculation of "s" in the
equation below include measurements for shrub cover at the individual points?

Yes.

> >Effort        :    86.00000

> >  ---------  -----------  -----------  --------------  ----------------------

> >    h(0)     0.27274E-03  0.82188E-05       3.01      0.25704E-03  0.28940E-03

> >  ---------  -----------  -----------  --------------  ----------------------

> >In the above equation for "s", what is "fcn"?  I plan to use an Excel
spreadsheet to do the calculations.  I am somewhat mathematically challenged, so
it would be great if you know Excel and can tell me the function in Excel that
corresponds to "fcn".

Fcn is short for function.  It's a bit obscure I agree.  Your shrub covariate is
a non-factor covariate - let's denote it's value at a particular point as z.
Then to evaluate Exp(fcn(A(3))), you calculate Exp(z*A(3)).  So, overall:
k(y)= 1 - Exp(-(y/[A(1)*exp(z*A(3))])**-A(2))

> >In the following equation for probability of detection, g(y)=key(y)[1+series
(y)]/key(0)[1+series(0)] what parameters do I use to calculate series(y)?  The
example in Distance/Help uses A(3), but that example does not include a
covariate.

You didn't have any series expansion terms in your model, judging from your
output above.  In this case k(0)=1, so you don't need the bottom line so k(y)=g
(y).

As an aside, the above parameter estimates appear to indicate that there is very
little effect of the habitat covariate (A(3), unless your habitat values are
very large numbers.  For example, if z=1x10^11, then exp(z*A(3)) is 1.00926.
Did AIC really select this model over one with no covariates?  Also, the values
of A(1) and A(2) seem to indicate a wide shoulder and then a steep drop off --
although "wide" is relative to the scale of your measurements.

Generally, I would advise you to keep it simple, and use those as
cutpoints.

> > 2. How should I take into consideration (if at all) that there are
> > buildings around me where birds are not sighted and most likely not
> > located?

If your points were randomly located (or a grid of points randomly
positioned) in the study area, there is no need whatsoever to take account
of areas where the habitat is unsuitable.  You obtain a valid estimate of
average density through your study area, and a valid estimate of total
abundance.  However, in an urban environment, you may have to offset many
points from where they should be.  In that case, as part of an exercise in
assessing how much bias this point displacement causes, you might want to
look at this issue.

> > 3. Should I run the analysis for all the urban points together? Or analyz=

e
> > each point separately (where a small sample size is inevitable)

It is usually not sensible to obtain estimates by individual point, and
certainly not sensible to carry out independent analyses of data from each
point.  Sometimes, estimates by point are used, for example as input to a
spatial model.  In this case, either a common detection function would be
fitted across points or a common detection function model would be assumed
across points but with point-specific covariates.  If the main aim is to
estimate density or abundance within the study area (or strata within the
study area), then you would include all points in a single analysis
(though you would have a data field in Distance indicating which data came
from which point, as the robust methods for estimating variance in
Distance requires this information).

> > One last thing=85 in choosing between two models (for the same data and
> > filter), where one has a lower AIC value but the other has a higher

> > p_value for its chi-test, how can I declare one model better fits the dat=

a
> > then the next (I am aware of model averaging)

In that circumstance, it is unlikely that there is much to choose between
the models.  I would check the fitted detection functions are ensure that
they are biologically realistic (e.g. fall in detectability isn't
unrealistically fast at any point).  In Distance, you can define more than
one model, and use the bootstrap to quantify variance, without having
to condition on the single 'best' model.  Hence the variance includes a
component for model uncertainty.

See Buckland et al. (2001), page 296, which refers to the work of Hiby and
Krishna (in press at the time -- now published in Biometrics 57, 727-731).  I
recommend reading the paper as it is short and clearly written.  Neverthess, in
summary:

There are two issues to consider.

The first is estimating the number of animals within the surveyed region.  Hiby
and Krishna showed that there is no problem here, so long as (a) rather than
perpendicular distance, one measures the shortest distance between the animal
and the curving transect, and (b) the line is not too "wiggly" (there should be
few curves with radius of curvature less than the distance within which most
animals are seen).  In your case, perhaps the line is almost straight, in which
case you will probably find that (a) perpendicular distance and shortest
distance are almost identical so using the former is no problem, and (b) is
satisfied without any problems.

The second issue is extrapolating from the number in the surveyed region to the
number in the study area.  Many curved transects are curved in terrestrial
surveys because they are on existing trails.  Then the region surveyed is not a
random sample of the study area and there is no statistical basis to extrapolate
the density in the surveyed region to that in the whole area.  In your case, if
your lines were laid out according to a randomized design (e.g., systematic
random), and departures from the designed line locations are likely to be
uncorrelated with animal density (i.e., you don't tend to get "pushed" into
regions of high density by undersea currents) then you can ignore this issue.
If you did survey the region nonrandomly, then you're going to have to go to
great lengths to get an unbiased estimate of density (see Buckland et al. or
Hiby and Krishna for more on this).

Hope this helps,

 - Len

messages.subject_clean: Is distance analysis appropriate for this problem?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sally, list,

I would guess that you will get better precision from distance sampling vs strip
transect, but the only way to be sure is to try it and see (i.e., try both and
compare the precisions).  The extra component of variation due to estimating the
detection function is usually small in line transects, especially with this many
sightings.  (You may have less than 2652 at the end of your line transect
analysis however as you probably will use a bit of truncation.)  That's why I
think the line transect will be more precise.

Either way, I'm not sure that it's valid to do a chi-squared as you described,
since this assumes that the unburned and burned samples are independent, when in
fact in many cases these come from the same transect.

For a strip transect analysis, you could perform a separate chi-square on each
transect, each with one degree of freedom, and then sum the chi-squares to get
an overall test.  Don't know what to do here if you have some transects that are
all in one type (e.g., all unburned).  Perhaps others have ideas here.

For a line transect analysis, you will probably fit a separate detection
function (or covariate) for burned/unburned so estimates of density by
burned/unburned within lines will not be independent.  Probably the best way to
get confidence limits/a test on for the difference in densities is to implement
a nonparametric bootstrap, outside of Distance.  For each bootstrap replicate,
you choose a sample of 26 lines with replacement (pooling all visits to the
lines if you're only intersted in an overall estimate of difference).  You then
divide the sample into the burned and unburned section of each line, and set
these up a strata in a distance data file.  You then call the Distance analysis
engine to estimate the detection function and give you estimates of density by
stratum, and store these.  Repeat many times.  The distribution of the
difference in stratum density estimates can be used to give you confidence
limits and a test on the difference.  Calling the Distance analysis engine in
this way has been discussed several times before on the list (search the
archives under "stand alone" or "analysis engine" or "simulation").

Hope this helps,

 - Len

messages.subject_clean: Ungulate line transects in large woodland areas
messages.body_plain:
Hi List,

with some colleagues, I am preparing a (ground) line transect survey on
ungulate population sizes in two reserves in Miombo woodland of W
Tanzania. The aim is to collect reliable and representative data for
more species - and possibly to obtain more precise estimates - than
previous aerial surveys (which did not use distance analysis). Since I
am still insecure whether we can achieve these goals, I hope to get some
advice from list members.

There are a certain number of difficulties that we are facing: (1) The
two areas for which we need estimates are fairly large (ca. 4,000 sq.km <http://sq.km>
each), and we therefore need to work with quite a number of field
technicians, (2) the areas are fairly heterogeneous in habitat type
(from open plains to closed woodland), (3) accessibility is limited to a
period of the year when waterlevels are low and plains are accessible,
but there are still several rivers and some steep escarpments which
cannot be crossed, (4) many species have clumped distributions with
large variance in cluster sizes (e.g. buffaloes), (5) there are no
permanent transects available.

We have only pre-study distance data from road transects. These roads
are not representative for the area but we probably need a minimum of
800 km survey effort in each of the reserves. We have a good number of
field staff (NP rangers) and we can use them for a period of four weeks
so would be able to obtain a fair amount of data during what we believe
is the best time of the year. However, we will not be able to survey
different strata extensively (e.g. plains vs. woods), and will need to
pool them in order to obtain a sufficient number of observations per
species (60-80).

We are presently dividing the area into different sectors due to
accessibility (rivers, escarpments), and - using GIS/Distance interface-
plan to place transects systematically within these sectors, with random
startpoints. We might need ca. 50 transects (15 km each). We plan to
train technicians (10 teams) in the field protocols. We would equip
survey teams with GPS, laser rangefinder and compass, and send them out
on straight 15 km transects which should be walked within one morning
(btw.7 and 11 A.M.). We plan to let them collect radial distances and
angles. Logistics should allow to place them at the starting point and
collect them at the end.

Does anybody know about similar large-scale line transect sampling in
savanna woodland (apart from aerial surveys)? I am happy about any
advice I can get, be it on the field design or practical organisation,

Matthias

messages.body_plain:
> > I'm using DISTANCE in my population study on tarsiers, comparing disturbed
> > and undisturbed forest sites.
> >
> > For each of the sites, I sampled 10 transects twice (once in either
> > direction and each set of ten, a few weeks apart). Is there a way of putting
> > in repeats or will I have to treat them as seperate transects of the site?

You'll find responses to very similar queries in the list archives.
When you survey each line twice, simply record the effort as twice the
line length.  If subsequent surveys were simply to get more data, and all
you need is average abundance over the time period, then do the same
again.  Thus if you walk a line 6 times, record effort as 6 times the
length.  If you recorded this as if it were 6 different transects, your
vairance estimate would be biased low, so you should not treat them as
separate transects.
